question: Find the exact terms and definitions the specifications use for Head-of-Line (HOL) blocking in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3: HTTP-layer vs transport-layer HOL; HTTP/2 connection, stream, frame, multiplexing, flow control, HPACK and its order dependence; QUIC streams, STREAM frame, per-stream ordering, QUIC flow control, HTTP/3 control and critical streams, QPACK encoder and decoder streams, dynamic table, blocked stream and SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS; and which RFC defines each term.

facts.summary: RFC 9113 says HTTP/1.0 allowed one outstanding request per TCP connection, and HTTP/1.1 pipelining only partly fixed concurrency and still suffers from application-layer head-of-line blocking.
facts.quote: HTTP/1.0 allowed only one request to be outstanding at a time on a given TCP [TCP] connection. HTTP/1.1 [HTTP/1.1] added request pipelining, but this only partially addressed request concurrency and still suffers from application-layer head-of-line blocking.

facts.summary: RFC 9113 states that HTTP/2 does not address TCP head-of-line blocking.
facts.quote: Note, however, that TCP head-of-line blocking is not addressed by this protocol.

facts.summary: HTTP/2 is described as a connection-oriented application-layer protocol running over a TCP connection, with the client as the TCP initiator.
facts.quote: HTTP/2 is a connection-oriented application-layer protocol that runs over a TCP connection ([TCP]). The client is the TCP connection initiator.

facts.summary: In HTTP/2, multiplexing means each request/response exchange gets its own stream; the overview calls streams largely independent so a stalled request does not block others.
facts.quote: Multiplexing of requests is achieved by having each HTTP request/response exchange associated with its own stream (Section 5). Streams are largely independent of each other, so a blocked or stalled request or response does not prevent progress on other streams.

facts.summary: RFC 9113 defines a connection as a transport-layer connection between two endpoints.
facts.quote: A transport-layer connection between two endpoints.

facts.summary: RFC 9113 defines a frame as the smallest unit of communication in an HTTP/2 connection: a header plus a variable-length octet sequence shaped by the frame type.
facts.quote: The smallest unit of communication within an HTTP/2 connection, consisting of a header and a variable-length sequence of octets structured according to the frame type.

facts.summary: RFC 9113 defines a stream as a bidirectional flow (independent sequence) of frames inside one HTTP/2 connection; one connection can hold many open streams whose frames are interleaved.
facts.quote: A "stream" is an independent, bidirectional sequence of frames exchanged between the client and server within an HTTP/2 connection. … A single HTTP/2 connection can contain multiple concurrently open streams, with either endpoint interleaving frames from multiple streams.

facts.summary: RFC 9113 says multiplexing streams over one TCP connection creates contention and blocked streams, and that flow control applies both per stream and to the whole connection.
facts.quote: Using streams for multiplexing introduces contention over use of the TCP connection, resulting in blocked streams. A flow-control scheme ensures that streams on the same connection do not destructively interfere with each other. Flow control is used for both individual streams and the connection as a whole.

facts.summary: HTTP/2 flow control is credit-based and uses WINDOW_UPDATE frames, with receivers advertising octets they accept per stream and per connection.
facts.quote: Flow control is based on WINDOW_UPDATE frames. Receivers advertise how many octets they are prepared to receive on a stream and for the entire connection. This is a credit-based scheme.

facts.summary: The initial HTTP/2 flow-control window is 65,535 octets for new streams and for the connection, and only DATA frames count against it.
facts.quote: The initial value for the flow-control window is 65,535 octets for both new streams and the overall connection. … only DATA frames are subject to flow control

facts.summary: RFC 9113 calls the process field section compression/decompression of field blocks, defers details to [COMPRESSION], and notes that document calls it header compression.
facts.quote: Field section compression is the process of compressing a set of field lines (Section 5.2 of [HTTP]) to form a field block. … Details of HTTP/2 field section compression and decompression are defined in [COMPRESSION], which, for historical reasons, refers to these processes as header compression and decompression.

facts.summary: The [COMPRESSION] reference in RFC 9113 is RFC 7541, HPACK: Header Compression for HTTP/2.
facts.quote: [COMPRESSION] … Peon, R. and H. Ruellan, "HPACK: Header Compression for HTTP/2", RFC 7541

facts.summary: A field block must be sent as a contiguous run of frames with no frames from other streams in between, and a receiver must end the connection with COMPRESSION_ERROR if it does not decompress a field block.
facts.quote: Each field block is processed as a discrete unit. Field blocks MUST be transmitted as a contiguous sequence of frames, with no interleaved frames of any other type or from any other stream. … A receiver MUST terminate the connection with a connection error (Section 5.4.1) of type COMPRESSION_ERROR if it does not decompress a field block.

facts.summary: HTTP/2 field compression is stateful: each endpoint has one HPACK encoder context and one decoder context for all field blocks on the connection, with the dynamic table as the main state.
facts.quote: Field compression is stateful. Each endpoint has an HPACK encoder context and an HPACK decoder context that are used for encoding and decoding all field blocks on a connection. Section 4 of [COMPRESSION] defines the dynamic table, which is the primary state for each context.

facts.summary: RFC 9000 defines a stream as a unidirectional or bidirectional channel of ordered bytes inside a QUIC connection, which can carry many streams at once.
facts.quote: A unidirectional or bidirectional channel of ordered bytes within a QUIC connection. A QUIC connection can carry multiple simultaneous streams.

facts.summary: RFC 9000 defines a QUIC frame as a unit of structured protocol information carried inside QUIC packets, with several frame types.
facts.quote: A unit of structured protocol information. There are multiple frame types, each of which carries different information. Frames are contained in QUIC packets.

facts.summary: QUIC streams may interleave data with other streams, and QUIC gives no way to order bytes across different streams.
facts.quote: Streams can be created by either endpoint, can concurrently send data interleaved with other streams, and can be canceled. QUIC does not provide any means of ensuring ordering between bytes on different streams.

facts.summary: Unidirectional streams carry data only from initiator to peer, bidirectional streams carry both ways, and bit 0x02 of the stream ID tells the two apart.
facts.quote: Unidirectional streams carry data in one direction: from the initiator of the stream to its peer. Bidirectional streams allow for data to be sent in both directions. … The second least significant bit (0x02) of the stream ID distinguishes between bidirectional streams (with the bit set to 0) and unidirectional streams (with the bit set to 1).

facts.summary: STREAM frames carry application data, and the receiver uses their Stream ID and Offset fields to put the data in order.
facts.quote: STREAM frames (Section 19.8) encapsulate data sent by an application. An endpoint uses the Stream ID and Offset fields in STREAM frames to place data in order.

facts.summary: An endpoint must deliver each stream to the application as an ordered byte stream, buffering out-of-order data up to the flow control limit; out-of-order delivery is an optional implementation feature.
facts.quote: Endpoints MUST be able to deliver stream data to an application as an ordered byte stream. Delivering an ordered byte stream requires that an endpoint buffer any data that is received out of order, up to the advertised flow control limit. … However, implementations MAY choose to offer the ability to deliver data out of order to a receiving application.

facts.summary: STREAM frames implicitly create a stream and carry its data; their frame type values run from 0x08 to 0x0f.
facts.quote: STREAM frames implicitly create a stream and carry stream data. The Type field in the STREAM frame takes the form 0b00001XXX (or the set of values from 0x08 to 0x0f).

facts.summary: QUIC flow control is limit-based with two levels: stream flow control per stream and connection flow control over all streams; senders must stay within both.
facts.quote: QUIC employs a limit-based flow control scheme where a receiver advertises the limit of total bytes it is prepared to receive on a given stream or for the entire connection. This leads to two levels of data flow control in QUIC: … Stream flow control, which prevents a single stream from consuming the entire receive buffer for a connection by limiting the amount of data that can be sent on each stream. … Connection flow control, which prevents senders from exceeding a receiver's buffer capacity for the connection by limiting the total bytes of stream data sent in STREAM frames on all streams. … Senders MUST NOT send data in excess of either limit.

facts.summary: Receivers raise QUIC flow-control limits with MAX_STREAM_DATA (per stream) and MAX_DATA (per connection) frames after the initial transport parameters.
facts.quote: A receiver sets initial limits for all streams through transport parameters during the handshake (Section 7.4). Subsequently, a receiver sends MAX_STREAM_DATA frames (Section 19.10) or MAX_DATA frames (Section 19.9) to the sender to advertise larger limits.

facts.summary: In QUIC flow control, a sender that has reached the limit is called blocked and should signal it with STREAM_DATA_BLOCKED or DATA_BLOCKED.
facts.quote: If a sender has sent data up to the limit, it will be unable to send new data and is considered blocked. A sender SHOULD send a STREAM_DATA_BLOCKED or DATA_BLOCKED frame to indicate to the receiver that it has data to write but is blocked by flow control limits.

facts.summary: QUIC multiplexes by interleaving STREAM frames in packets; it avoids HOL blocking across streams since a lost packet blocks only streams with data in it, but all streams in that packet are blocked.
facts.quote: Stream multiplexing is achieved by interleaving STREAM frames from multiple streams into one or more QUIC packets. … One of the benefits of QUIC is avoidance of head-of-line blocking across multiple streams. When a packet loss occurs, only streams with data in that packet are blocked waiting for a retransmission to be received, while other streams can continue making progress. Note that when data from multiple streams is included in a single QUIC packet, loss of that packet blocks all those streams from making progress.

facts.summary: RFC 9000 cites [QUIC-RECOVERY] as RFC 9002, QUIC Loss Detection and Congestion Control.
facts.quote: [QUIC-RECOVERY] … Iyengar, J., Ed. and I. Swett, Ed., "QUIC Loss Detection and Congestion Control", RFC 9002

facts.summary: RFC 9114 says HTTP/2 multiplexing is invisible to TCP loss recovery, so a lost or reordered packet stalls all active transactions, even those not hit by the loss.
facts.quote: HTTP/2 ([HTTP/2]) introduced a binary framing and multiplexing layer to improve latency without modifying the transport layer. However, because the parallel nature of HTTP/2's multiplexing is not visible to TCP's loss recovery mechanisms, a lost or reordered packet causes all active transactions to experience a stall regardless of whether that transaction was directly impacted by the lost packet.

facts.summary: QUIC brings stream multiplexing and per-stream flow control, and HTTP/3 relies on it for reliable, in-order, per-stream delivery.
facts.quote: The QUIC transport protocol incorporates stream multiplexing and per-stream flow control, similar to that provided by the HTTP/2 framing layer. … HTTP/3 relies on QUIC to provide confidentiality and integrity protection of data; peer authentication; and reliable, in-order, per-stream delivery.

facts.summary: In HTTP/3 each request-response pair uses one QUIC stream, connection-wide frames go on a dedicated control stream, and the overview calls streams independent so loss on one does not stop the others.
facts.quote: Frames that apply to the entire connection are conveyed on a dedicated control stream. … Each request-response pair consumes a single QUIC stream. Streams are independent of each other, so one stream that is blocked or suffers packet loss does not prevent progress on other streams.

facts.summary: HTTP/3 replaces HPACK with QPACK because HPACK relies on in-order transmission, which QUIC does not guarantee; QPACK modifies table state on separate unidirectional streams.
facts.quote: Because HPACK ([HPACK]) relies on in-order transmission of compressed field sections (a guarantee not provided by QUIC), HTTP/3 replaces HPACK with QPACK ([QPACK]). QPACK uses separate unidirectional streams to modify and track field table state, while encoded field sections refer to the state of the table without modifying it.

facts.summary: RFC 9114 defines stream as a bytestream from QUIC; every stream in an HTTP/3 connection is an HTTP/3 stream, and there are several stream types.
facts.quote: A bidirectional or unidirectional bytestream provided by the QUIC transport. All streams within an HTTP/3 connection can be considered "HTTP/3 streams", but multiple stream types are defined within HTTP/3.

facts.summary: An HTTP/3 frame is the smallest unit of communication on a stream; RFC 9114 prefixes transport frames with QUIC to tell them apart.
facts.quote: The smallest unit of communication on a stream in HTTP/3, consisting of a header and a variable-length sequence of bytes structured according to the frame type. … Where frames from [QUIC-TRANSPORT] are referenced, the frame name will be prefaced with "QUIC".

facts.summary: RFC 9114 says QPACK, a variant of HPACK, lets the encoder control how much head-of-line blocking compression can cause, trading compression efficiency against latency.
facts.quote: [QPACK] describes a variation of HPACK that gives an encoder some control over how much head-of-line blocking can be caused by compression. This allows an encoder to balance compression efficiency with latency.

facts.summary: A QUIC stream delivers its own bytes reliably and in order but gives no ordering relative to other streams; QUIC STREAM framing is hidden from HTTP/3, which does not use out-of-order delivery.
facts.quote: A QUIC stream provides reliable in-order delivery of bytes, but makes no guarantees about order of delivery with regard to bytes on other streams. In version 1 of QUIC, the stream data containing HTTP frames is carried by QUIC STREAM frames, but this framing is invisible to the HTTP framing layer. … Although QUIC permits out-of-order delivery within a stream, HTTP/3 does not make use of this feature.

facts.summary: In HTTP/3, all client-initiated bidirectional streams carry requests and responses and are called request streams.
facts.quote: All client-initiated bidirectional streams are used for HTTP requests and responses. A bidirectional stream ensures that the response can be readily correlated with the request. These streams are referred to as request streams.

facts.summary: Each endpoint needs a control stream and QPACK needs two more unidirectional streams, so transport parameters must allow at least three; these are called the critical unidirectional streams and should be created first.
facts.quote: Each endpoint needs to create at least one unidirectional stream for the HTTP control stream. QPACK requires two additional unidirectional streams, and other extensions might require further streams. Therefore, the transport parameters sent by both clients and servers MUST allow the peer to create at least three unidirectional streams. … creating the critical unidirectional streams. Endpoints SHOULD create the HTTP control stream as well as the unidirectional streams required by mandatory extensions (such as the QPACK encoder and decoder streams) first

facts.summary: The control stream has stream type 0x00, and closing either control stream at any point is a connection error of type H3_CLOSED_CRITICAL_STREAM.
facts.quote: A control stream is indicated by a stream type of 0x00. … If either control stream is closed at any point, this MUST be treated as a connection error of type H3_CLOSED_CRITICAL_STREAM.

facts.summary: H3_CLOSED_CRITICAL_STREAM, code 0x0104, means a stream the HTTP/3 connection requires was closed or reset.
facts.quote: H3_CLOSED_CRITICAL_STREAM (0x0104): … A stream required by the HTTP/3 connection was closed or reset.

facts.summary: RFC 9114's normative references map [QPACK] to RFC 9204 and [QUIC-TRANSPORT] to RFC 9000.
facts.quote: [QPACK] … "QPACK: Field Compression for HTTP/3", RFC 9204 … [QUIC-TRANSPORT] … "QUIC: A UDP-Based Multiplexed and Secure Transport", RFC 9000

facts.summary: RFC 9114's informative references map [HPACK] to RFC 7541 and [HTTP/2] to RFC 9113.
facts.quote: [HPACK] … "HPACK: Header Compression for HTTP/2", RFC 7541 … [HTTP/2] … "HTTP/2", RFC 9113

facts.summary: RFC 9204 defines QPACK as the field compression format for HTTP/3, a variant of HPACK meant to reduce head-of-line blocking.
facts.quote: This specification defines QPACK: a compression format for efficiently representing HTTP fields that is to be used in HTTP/3. This is a variation of HPACK compression that seeks to reduce head-of-line blocking.

facts.summary: HPACK (RFC 7541) assumes a total ordering of frames across all streams, so using it in HTTP/3 would cause HOL blocking; QPACK is redesigned to stay correct under out-of-order delivery.
facts.quote: HTTP/2 uses HPACK ([RFC7541]) for compression of the header and trailer sections. If HPACK were used for HTTP/3 ([HTTP/3]), it would induce head-of-line blocking for field sections due to built-in assumptions of a total ordering across frames on all streams. … QPACK reuses core concepts from HPACK, but is redesigned to allow correctness in the presence of out-of-order delivery, with flexibility for implementations to balance between resilience against head-of-line blocking and optimal compression ratio.

facts.summary: RFC 9204 defines a field section as an ordered collection of HTTP field lines belonging to one HTTP message.
facts.quote: An ordered collection of HTTP field lines associated with an HTTP message.

facts.summary: RFC 9204 defines the encoder as what encodes field sections, the decoder as what decodes them, and Insert Count as the total entries inserted in the dynamic table.
facts.quote: Encoder: … An implementation that encodes field sections. … Decoder: … An implementation that decodes encoded field sections. … Insert Count: … The total number of entries inserted in the dynamic table.

facts.summary: References to the static table or literals never risk HOL blocking; references to the dynamic table do when the encoder has no acknowledgment that the entry reached the decoder.
facts.quote: References to the static table and literal representations do not require any dynamic state and never risk head-of-line blocking. References to the dynamic table risk head-of-line blocking if the encoder has not received an acknowledgment indicating the entry is available at the decoder.

facts.summary: Since QUIC gives no ordering across streams, a decoder can see a reference to a dynamic table entry not yet received; a stream whose Required Insert Count exceeds the decoder's Insert Count is called blocked.
facts.quote: Because QUIC does not guarantee order between data on different streams, a decoder might encounter a representation that references a dynamic table entry that it has not yet received. … When the decoder receives an encoded field section with a Required Insert Count greater than its own Insert Count, the stream cannot be processed immediately and is considered "blocked"

facts.summary: Required Insert Count is carried in each encoded field section and is the lowest Insert Count with which that section can be decoded.
facts.quote: Each encoded field section contains a Required Insert Count (Section 4.5.1), the lowest possible value for the Insert Count with which the field section can be decoded.

facts.summary: The decoder caps blocked streams with SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS; the encoder must always stay within it, and exceeding it is a QPACK_DECOMPRESSION_FAILED connection error.
facts.quote: The decoder specifies an upper bound on the number of streams that can be blocked using the SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS setting; see Section 5. An encoder MUST limit the number of streams that could become blocked to the value of SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS at all times. If a decoder encounters more blocked streams than it promised to support, it MUST treat this as a connection error of type QPACK_DECOMPRESSION_FAILED.

facts.summary: In QPACK, encoded field sections and encoder-stream instructions travel on separate streams, unlike HPACK, whose header blocks themselves carry the dynamic table updates.
facts.quote: Note that encoded field sections and encoder stream instructions arrive on separate streams. This is unlike HPACK, where encoded field sections (header blocks) can contain instructions that modify the dynamic table, and there is no dedicated stream of HPACK instructions.

facts.summary: Blocked data should stay inside the blocked stream's flow-control window; the stream unblocks once Insert Count reaches the Required Insert Count of every section started on it.
facts.quote: While blocked, encoded field section data SHOULD remain in the blocked stream's flow-control window. This data is unusable until the stream becomes unblocked, and releasing the flow control prematurely makes the decoder vulnerable to memory exhaustion attacks. A stream becomes unblocked when the Insert Count becomes greater than or equal to the Required Insert Count for all encoded field sections the decoder has started reading from the stream.

facts.summary: The QPACK dynamic table is a FIFO list of field lines shared by encoder and decoder, starting empty, filled by encoder-stream instructions.
facts.quote: The dynamic table consists of a list of field lines maintained in first-in, first-out order. A QPACK encoder and decoder share a dynamic table that is initially empty. The encoder adds entries to the dynamic table and sends them to the decoder via instructions on the encoder stream

facts.summary: The encoder stream is unidirectional stream type 0x02 carrying encoder instructions; the decoder stream is type 0x03 carrying decoder instructions back.
facts.quote: An encoder stream is a unidirectional stream of type 0x02. It carries an unframed sequence of encoder instructions from encoder to decoder. … A decoder stream is a unidirectional stream of type 0x03. It carries an unframed sequence of decoder instructions from decoder to encoder.

facts.summary: Each endpoint may open at most one encoder and one decoder stream, must not close them, and closing either is an H3_CLOSED_CRITICAL_STREAM connection error.
facts.quote: Each endpoint MUST initiate, at most, one encoder stream and, at most, one decoder stream. … Closure of either unidirectional stream type MUST be treated as a connection error of type H3_CLOSED_CRITICAL_STREAM.

facts.summary: QPACK adds two HTTP/3 settings: SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY (0x01, the counterpart of HTTP/2 SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE) and SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS (0x07), both defaulting to zero.
facts.quote: SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY (0x01): … The default value is zero. See Section 3.2 for usage. This is the equivalent of the SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE from HTTP/2. … SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS (0x07): … The default value is zero. See Section 2.1.2.

conflicts.topic: does packet loss on one HTTP/3 stream leave the other streams unaffected?
conflicts.note: RFC 9114 overview says independent streams are not held up by loss on another; RFC 9000 adds the condition that loss of a packet carrying several streams blocks all of them

conflicts.topic: are HTTP/3 streams free of head-of-line blocking?
conflicts.note: RFC 9114 overview calls streams independent; RFC 9204 says a stream can be blocked waiting for dynamic table entries sent on the encoder stream

conflicts.topic: does a blocked HTTP/2 stream stall the others?
conflicts.note: RFC 9113 overview says streams are largely independent; RFC 9114 says a lost or reordered TCP packet stalls all active HTTP/2 transactions (RFC 9113 F2 also says TCP HOL is not addressed)
